title: Soft Actor–Critic With Loop‐Aware Detection and Event‐Triggered Stochastic Escape
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes soft actor–critic with loop‐aware detection and event‐triggered stochastic escape. This is a reinforcement‐learning navigation algorithm for mobile robots operating in complex, unknown environments. The algorithm builds on soft actor–critic (SAC) and adds two cooperative modules. First, the real‐time loop detector can spot local optima traps during operation. It does this by checking the similarity of the robot's path over time and space, and by monitoring how often the robot changes direction in straight‐line speed. Frequent changes can cause the robot to move back and forth. When loops are detected, dynamic penalties guide the robot out of these traps. Second, the event‐triggered stochastic escape (ETSE) mechanism solves deadlocks in complex terrain. When the algorithm detects repetitive back‐and‐forth motions, the ETSE takes control. It injects high‐amplitude stochastic perturbations into the control signals to disrupt the deadlocked dynamics. This physical intervention physically forces the robot out of local minima and helps when normal reward signals do not guide learning. In Gazebo simulations, our method outperforms SAC, TD3, and DDPG in static and dynamic scenarios. Results show it adapts well and is robust in complex environments, providing a new lightweight option for autonomous robot navigation.

title: Beyond Light Cones: State Preparation Complexity in Quantum Spin Glasses
abstract: We introduce a method for studying state preparation complexity in dense quantum $p$-spin Hamiltonians on $n$ qubits, going beyond bounds based only on circuit lightcones. The key input is the class's effective profile complexity, which is derived from the metric entropy of its Pauli profiles. These profiles record expectations of all Pauli operators supported on exactly $p$ qubits. Classes with uniformly bounded quadratic effective profile complexity remain separated from the ground-state energy by a positive multiple of $\sqrt n$ for sufficiently large fixed $p$. At subquadratic effective profile complexity, the class cannot outperform a suitable benchmark class at leading order, with product states providing a universal benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem of Berta et al. (arXiv:1810.12197) with Gaussian process entropy bounds. Applying this framework, we show that attaining near-ground-state energy requires $Ω(n^2/\log n)$ one- and two-qubit gates, even with arbitrary discardable ancillas. We also obtain depth-width tradeoffs, entanglement-depth and matrix product state bond-dimension lower bounds, and obstructions for both orientations at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966), with total circuit width $O(n)$. In first-level reverse magic, a shallow circuit is followed by an unrestricted Clifford circuit. The latter can spread local observables across the system, preventing a direct application of small-lightcone bounds. For this first-level class, our bounds also allow arbitrarily many clean ancillas at fixed shallow-circuit depth. A sharper benchmark shows that Clifford+$T$ circuits with $o(n)$ $T$-gates have no leading-order energy advantage over product stabilizer states, even with unrestricted Clifford operations and arbitrary discardable ancillas.

title: Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for video generation usually assigns one scalar reward to an entire sampled video. Yet a video is not uniformly flawed: some visual tokens may already satisfy the prompt, whereas others require correction. A scalar reward cannot localize errors, causing optimization to perturb satisfactory tokens while under-targeting the tokens that actually need to change. We introduce Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning, TVRL, a framework that derives token-level credit from the reward being optimized. Our key insight is that the answer likelihood of a frozen vision-language model provides both signals: its outputs contribute to the video-level reward, while magnitudes of its video-input gradients reveal which generated video tokens most affect that score. We instantiate TVRL in Group Relative Policy Optimization by averaging prompt-derived question rewards into one group-relative advantage and using detached, question-conditioned token-credit maps to reweight dense denoising-transition log-probabilities inside the clipped policy ratio. On VBench-2.0, TVRL achieves an Overall score of 57.69, outperforming the base model by 3.60 points. TVRL also improves matched GRPO baselines across three SDE samplers (SAGE, Flow, and Dance) by 2.68--3.15 points and across four reward models (VideoAlign, VideoScore2, UnifiedReward2, and Qwen3.5-9B) by 1.33--3.15 points.

title: Higher-Order Positional Encodings for Graph Representation Learning
abstract: Many real-world systems exhibit higher-order interactions among groups of entities that cannot be captured by pairwise relationships alone. Graph Transformers and Graph Neural Networks increasingly rely on positional encodings to enrich graph representations, yet existing positional encodings are computed solely from the original graph and therefore cannot directly capture observed higher-order interactions. Topological Deep Learning addresses this limitation by lifting graphs to simplicial complexes, but typically requires performing message passing or attention on higher-order neural network representations. We introduce a representation learning paradigm that enriches graph representations with higher-order topology through positional encodings, enabling standard graph learning models to exploit lifted incidence structure without modifying the backbone. We derive a theoretical characterization of the expressivity of higher-order positional encodings, proving that node-level operators induced by higher-order lifts can mix graph Laplacian frequencies in ways that scalar graph spectral filters cannot. Guided by this theory, we instantiate higher-order positional encodings using Hodge Laplacians derived from clique complexes. Experiments with Graph Transformers on ZINC and controlled synthetic benchmarks demonstrate improvements in predictive performance, while a fixed-1-skeleton experiment shows that the pipeline can transmit higher-order information when cells are supplied independently of the graph. Together, our results establish higher-order positional encodings as a principled bridge between graph positional encodings and topological deep learning.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of First-Order Noisy Input Gaussian Process Regression under Increasing Input Uncertainty
abstract: Gaussian Process (GP) regression provides a flexible probabilistic framework for learning nonlinear input--output relationships, but standard formulations typically assume that input variables are observed without error. Noisy Input Gaussian Process Regression (NIGP) addresses this limitation by propagating input uncertainty through a first-order Taylor approximation of the GP posterior mean, thereby introducing an input-dependent effective variance. This study presents a systematic empirical evaluation of the established first-order NIGP formulation under progressively increasing input uncertainty rather than proposing a new mathematical correction. Synthetic experiments were conducted using a sine--trend function with input-noise standard deviations ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 and 50 paired Monte Carlo replicates per condition. Performance was assessed using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Negative Log Predictive Density (NLPD), Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP), absolute coverage error (ACE), mean prediction interval width (MPIW), Winkler score, and Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). The first-order approximation was additionally evaluated against Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation and a second-order Taylor reference, while further experiments examined multiple nonlinear benchmarks, heterogeneous input uncertainty, and multidimensional correlated input noise. In the principal experiment, GP and NIGP exhibited similar point-prediction performance at low input-noise levels, whereas NIGP produced substantially lower RMSE and MAE from $\sigma_x=0.4$ onward, with the largest differences occurring at high noise levels. At $\sigma_x=1.0$, mean RMSE decreased from 2.10461 for GP to 0.35937 for NIGP, while mean MAE decreased from 1.59203 to 0.29728. The corresponding bias--variance analysis showed that these improvements were associated with reductions in both predictive bias and variance. Probabilistic performance was noise-dependent: the models were broadly similar at low noise levels, while NIGP produced substantially narrower intervals and lower NLPD, Winkler, and CRPS values at higher noise levels. However, its coverage relative to the nominal 95\% level was not uniformly improved. The first-order approximation also deteriorated as input noise increased, with mean relative error rising from approximately 2.1\% at $\sigma_x=0.1$ to 75.8\% at $\sigma_x=1.0$, while empirical convergence of the iterative procedure declined from 100\% to 34\%. The results demonstrate that the empirical benefits of NIGP become increasingly evident under moderate-to-high input uncertainty, but its effectiveness remains constrained by the accuracy of the first-order approximation and the numerical stability of the iterative uncertainty-propagation procedure.

title: Timeless intelligence: what doesn’t age in the age of ai
abstract: 1988. Antalya Bus Terminal. A thirteen-year-old girl, alone, boards the bus to İzmir. No one in her immediate family has graduated from university. There is no map, and no role model to follow. Nearly forty years later, she has been a partner at Accenture and IBM, delivering technology transformations across more than twenty-five countries, led a retail transformation now taught as a case at Harvard Business School, and founded an AI startup factory for one of Türkiye's oldest and largest banks - often as the only woman, or the only foreigner, at the table. Timeless Intelligence began as a letter to her two sons. It became a guide for anyone standing at a threshold: a first job, a new role, a world where AI can write the report and the presentation too. Tools change. Four things don’t: action, curiosity, resilience and authenticity. In sixteen short chapters, each built on a real moment from her life, Karakullukçu shows how these four cornerstones are laid, and how to use AI as a mirror, not an answer machine. Everyone will have the same tools. The difference will be the person using them. To verify before print: “one of Türkiye’s oldest and largest banks” Barış Karakullukçu is a former Accenture partner, the former CEO of the Turkish retailer Mudo, whose transformation is a Harvard Business School case, and the founder of an AI startup factory. She chairs Türkiye's AI and Technology Association and TÜBİSAD's AI Committee, serves on corporate boards and teaches as a guest lecturer at universities. She lives in Istanbul with her husband and two sons.

title: Do Cook: Interventions for Answering Counterfactuals in Policy Graphs
abstract: XAI is a field of research focused on extracting explanations from AI models. Explanations have a causal facet to them, and the word ‘counterfactual’ is often floated around when discussing explanations. Counterfactuals, however, are concepts that exist in a very high level of the causal hierarchy, while most methods are observational and correlation-based: the old adage of ‘correlation is not causation’ rings a bell. To reach the level of counterfactuals, interventions are needed. In this paper, we extend Intention Policy Graphs with interventional information. This allows answering previously unanswerable alternative-action queries, enabling the framework to answer counterfactual questions within its state-based abstraction. We propose strategies for gathering this information.

title: PENERAPAN ALGORITMA K-NEAREST NEIGHBOR (KNN) UNTUK ANALISIS SENTIMEN PUBLIK TERHADAP SHOPPE
abstract: Media sosial, khususnya Twitter, menjadi sarana penting bagi masyarakat dalam menyampaikan pendapat dan pengalaman mereka terhadap layanan e-commerce seperti Shopee. Informasi yang tersaji dalam bentuk cuitan mengandung sentimen yang dapat dianalisis untuk memahami persepsi publik. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menerapkan algoritma K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) dalam menganalisis sentimen pengguna Twitter terhadap Shopee. Data diperoleh dari cuitan yang relevan, kemudian diproses melalui tahapan preprocessing yang meliputi pembersihan data, penyeragaman huruf, tokenisasi, stemming, serta penghapusan stopword. Data teks selanjutnya direpresentasikan dalam bentuk numerik menggunakan metode Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) sebelum dilakukan klasifikasi sentimen. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa algoritma KNN menghasilkan performa klasifikasi yang sangat baik, dengan nilai akurasi, precision, recall, dan F1-score mencapai 1,00 pada seluruh kelas sentimen. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi TF-IDF dan KNN efektif digunakan dalam analisis sentimen data media sosial berbahasa Indonesia.

title: Propagation criteria for Boolean functions associated to bipartite Cayley graphs
abstract: Abstract In this paper we consider the issues of synthesis and analysis of parameterized classes of Boolean functions that are asymptotically good with respect to the propagation criterion. The design of such classes is based on the construction proposed by A. Bernasconi and B. Codenotti in 2000. The construction uses the bipartite Cayley graph of a Boolean function. We present a constructive description of classes of Boolean functions that are asymptotically good with respect to the propagation criterion, investigate the basic properties of such classes and obtain lower bounds on class cardinalities.

title: What AR Glasses Leak: Physical Scene Inference from Encrypted Traffic
abstract: Augmented reality (AR) glasses continuously offload their view of the physical world to edge servers for rendering, and while this uplink is encrypted, its metadata is not: packet sizes, inter-packet intervals, and frame timing. Because video compression assigns bits based on visual complexity, motion, and scene structure, the resulting packet sizes and timing patterns can carry traces of the physical scene being captured. This creates an unusual side channel: it reveals the user's physical environment, independent of the app being used, to a passive on-path observer without needing to decrypt payloads, execute code on the device, or share physical proximity with the user. We show that leakage in an AR edge-offload uplink is strong enough to support classification of the AR user's physical scene type across different environments. Our results further reveal that scene information is distributed across multiple features rather than being concentrated in a single one. This explains what we observed when evaluating countermeasures: injecting jitter or padding alone is insufficient, because each defense only disrupts part of the leakage. Even when combined, these defenses face a practical tradeoff. Obscuring this leakage imposes latency and bandwidth overhead that directly conflicts with quality of service, revealing a persistent tension between privacy and real-time performance in edge-assisted AR.

title: Assignment Has Never Existed: Programs Have Always Been Difference Equations
abstract: The assignment statement x = x + 1 is a difference equation with its time index removed. Program verification research has shown that restoring the index simplifies reasoning, but only specification languages have incorporated this idea.

title: Unpacking colorectal TSR: Isolating the sources of discrepancy between human and AI assessment
abstract: The tumour-stroma ratio (TSR) is an established prognostic biomarker in colorectal cancer, yet manual scoring remains subject to interobserver variability. Automated methods have been proposed to improve reproducibility, but have been shown to produce different TSR scores than pathologists. The sources of this discrepancy have never been isolated and its underlying causes remain unknown. This work decomposes TSR scoring into ROI selection and TSR quantification and compares manual to automated scoring through five sequential questions. These questions cover: tissue segmentation, TSR quantification within a fixed ROI, TSR scoring in pathologist-selected ROIs, ROI selection, and the complete automated pipeline. The tissue segmentation model reached Dice scores of 0.896 for tumour and 0.837 for tumour stroma, the two classes from which the TSR is directly computed, on a clinically representative internal test set. Across all tissue classes, mean Dice scores of 0.860 and 0.870 were obtained on the public CRC-VAL-HE-7K and NCT-CRC-HE-100K datasets, respectively. Within predefined ROIs, manual quantification agreed less closely with an annotation-derived reference standard than automated quantification (mean κ = 0.60 versus 0.84; ρ = 0.85 versus 0.98), reflecting underestimation of stroma by most pathologists. When pathologists selected guideline-compliant ROIs, automated scores fell slightly outside the distribution of manual scores but showed a trend towards reduced dispersion, improving reproducibility at the cost of an upward offset that was largest in stroma-low cases. Fully automated TSR produced substantially higher scores than manual consensus (24.6 percentage points). Restricting the analysis to cases where pathologists preferred the automated ROI did not reduce the discrepancy, indicating that the quality of automated ROIs alone cannot explain the divergence. Scoring the automatically selected ROIs manually showed that ROI selection accounted for approximately 10 of the 24 percentage points of discrepancy, with the remaining 14 attributable to automated quantification. Despite this inflation, case ranking was largely preserved, but recalibrating the cut-off only partly restored agreement (maximum κ = 0.62 at 81%), as the difference between methods depended on observer and region and was most variable near the new cut-off. Automated pipelines excel at following explicit scoring rules. Pathologists apply implicit, experience-driven criteria that remain uncodified. These unspoken conventions may contribute to the established prognostic value of manual TSR. Comprehensive survival studies are needed to determine whether automated TSR is a valid substitute for manual TSR and whether it captures the same biological construct. Fully data-driven prognostic models, unconstrained by human scoring rules, may offer greater robustness and scalability.

title: Intelligent real-time traffic classification in SDN using deep learning
abstract: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enables programmable, centralized control of network forwarding, but effective controller applications depend on timely and reliable identification of heterogeneous traffic flows. This study evaluates a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network-Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) classifier for flow-level traffic classification in an SDN test environment. The CNN component learns discriminative feature patterns, while the LSTM component models temporal dependencies. CICIDS 2017 and controlled SDN traffic support the supervised classification experiment, while MAWI traces are used as background backbone traffic context rather than as a source of the five supervised labels. A balanced 500-flow diagnostic test subset (100 flows per class) yields 91.2% overall accuracy, macro-precision of 91.2%, macro-recall of 91.2%, and macro-F1 of 91.2%; malicious traffic achieves recall of 0.91 and F1-score of 0.901. Average model inference latency ranges from 1.1 to 2.3 ms across the reported traffic classes. The results show that the CNN-LSTM model provides a strong classification-performance/latency trade-off for real-time SDN traffic analysis. The classifier supplies traffic labels to the controller-facing policy layer, where they can inform downstream routing, queueing, or prioritization decisions. Because the experimental results reported here evaluate classification and model inference rather than a full before-and-after routing benchmark, network-level load-balancing gains are treated as a deployment implication rather than as a directly measured outcome. The study therefore contributes an internally consistent flow-classification evaluation together with an SDN-oriented integration pathway and clearly defined directions for controller-level validation.

title: Bayesian Supervised Learning Methods: Regularization and Predictive Uncertainty
abstract: Bayesian formulations of supervised learning methods differ in their prior distributions, inferential procedures, and treatment of predictive uncertainty. In this paper, we present a review of regularized regression, nearest-neighbor methods, support vector machines, tree ensembles, generalized additive models, Gaussian processes, and neural networks. The main objective is to examine the relationship between classical estimation procedures and their Bayesian formulations, with particular attention to posterior prediction. We consider likelihood- and loss-based updating, fixed and estimated hyperparameters, posterior integration, and computational approximations. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation is distinguished from posterior uncertainty, empirical Bayes from cross-validation-based tuning, and generalized updating from approximations to a likelihood-based posterior. The methods are compared in terms of calibration, prior sensitivity, model misspecification, interpretability, and scalability. Available software is described in a dated inventory. An illustrative comparison is performed in R using a real data set on concrete compressive strength, with common composition-grouped validation folds. Predictive accuracy, proper scoring rules, calibration, interval coverage, and computational cost are evaluated, and the approximation and numerical diagnostics are reported for each procedure. The discussion and numerical results indicate that predictive uncertainty depends on both model specification and inference; a Bayesian formulation alone does not ensure empirical calibration.

title: Tropical Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models typically maximizes expected return, adding up the probabilities of all successful trajectories. However, the classical sum formulation can only report how often the model policy succeeds, not which solution actually worked, and because probabilities sum to one, reinforcing one solution can make the model forget another that was never shown to be wrong. This makes expected return a poor fit for compositional reasoning, where a solution must be assembled from reasoning steps that the model produces in separate, often failed, attempts but rarely produces together. To address this, we propose Tropical Reinforcement Learning, which rests on a simple change of algebra: instead of adding the probabilities of alternative solutions, we take their maximum, which yields the tropical semiring. The value of a state then becomes the log-probability of its most likely verified solution, together with an explicit path that can be replayed and reused. This enables true composition, since the best prefix and the best suffix meeting at a shared state can be joined even when they come from different rollouts. To put this into practice, we introduce TROPIC, a training algorithm for deterministic, resettable environments with verifiable outcomes. On four agentic tasks (Sokoban, Countdown, FrozenLake, WebShop), TROPIC outperforms the strongest on-policy baselines by up to 16 percentage points. Changing the algebra of reinforcement learning, not just its estimators, can thus substantially improve compositional reasoning in language models

title: Counterfactual Auditing of Bias in Open-Source Large Language Models for Clinical Triage
abstract: Emergency department (ED) triage is a high-stakes prioritization task in which demographic, socioeconomic, and system-context information may improperly influence acuity assignment. Although open-source large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for local and privacy-preserving clinical decision support, it remains unclear how counterfactual bias varies across model families, sizes, medical-domain models, and domain-adapted models. We present a comparative counterfactual audit of ten open-source LLMs for pediatric Emergency Severity Index (ESI) prediction. Starting from real and handbook-style clinical vignettes, we construct paired counterfactual variants that change only one injected demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare-access, behavioral, social, or system-context variable while holding the clinical presentation fixed. Models include Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, a QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, MedGemma variants, MedLLaMA2-7B, GPT-OSS-20B, and GPT-OSS-120B. We measure any counterfactual shift, undertriage, overtriage, shifts greater than one ESI level, mean shift, and mean absolute shift. Counterfactual sensitivity varied substantially and did not consistently decrease with larger model size or medical-domain pretraining. evidence.abstract: Emergency department (ED) triage is a high-stakes prioritization task in which demographic, socioeconomic, and system-context information may improperly influence acuity assignment. Several larger or medical-domain models showed more significant shifts. Stratified and correlation analyses further revealed clinically important directionality and shared failure patterns hidden by aggregate rates. title: A Deterministic and Auditable AI Security Risk Assessment Framework with ATLAS Aligned Executable Rules and Formal Verification
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high impact and safety critical settings, yet security assessment remains difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches often rely on narrative checklists or assessor driven scoring, and they lack an explicit, machine evaluable mapping from observable engineering artefacts to stable technique level outcomes. We present an evidence driven AI security assessment framework that operationalises assessment as a deterministic decision function. The framework normalises heterogeneous artefacts into a project independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four level ordinal scale, compiles technique level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation to control mapping, and outputs technique indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links back to the triggering evidence. We package all normative choices as a versioned assessment policy object to support repeatable reassessment across snapshots. To ensure semantic correctness, we formally verify boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator over the full declared score domain. We evaluate the framework on five public open source AI projects pinned to explicit repository snapshots, quantify before and after changes under a unified hardening intervention, and validate responsiveness to real engineering changes through fork based implementations of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation and Continuous integration (CI) security scanning gates. Results show consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened observable controls, while worst case residual feasibility persists when technique specific core controls remain absent from the evidence scope.

title: Distillation of Tabular Foundation Models into Efficient Predictors
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve strong predictive performance through in-context learning, yet repeatedly conditioning on labeled data makes inference expensive. Knowledge distillation can reduce this cost by transferring their predictive ability to lightweight, dataset-specific students. However, the dependence of TFM predictions on both a labeled context and a query introduces two design questions: how to construct teacher supervision and whether expanding query coverage improves distillation. We examine these questions across two TFMs and both neural and tree-based students, and derive an effective distillation recipe. The recipe uses the full labeled training set as teacher context and trains students solely on teacher predictions for observed and synthetic queries. On TabArena, the resulting students outperform their supervised trained tuned-and-ensembled counterparts by 57-98 Elo points. Applied unchanged to TALENT, the same recipe improves matched default students on 236-258 of 300 datasets and reduces median primary error by 4.0-6.4%. The distilled students also achieve median inference speedups of 3.0-21.6 times over their teachers, offering a practical trade-off between predictive performance and repeated inference cost. Code is available at https://github.com/nums-ai/TFM_Distillation .

title: Sentence Specificity Scores for Collaborative Technical Documentation: A Domain-Transfer Study
abstract: Collaboration depends on shared context, and technical documentation is one way that context persists across people and AI teammates. Specificity, the amount and exactness of detail expressed in language, shapes what information documentation captures and how precisely that information is communicated. This work audits sentence-specificity scoring artifacts on technical documentation and tests whether scores applied only after generation help choose among fixed LLM-generated revisions. Across Wikipedia and three technical-documentation corpora, the fixed general-domain predictor SpeciTeller and the pinned post-publication author-repository implementation of Ko et al.'s target-adapted predictor produce different corpus orders and same-sentence rank agreement from -0.066 to 0.510. Strict filtering and token-length adjustment change these patterns without reconciling them. In the Gemma set, SpeciTeller ranking raises direction-valid selection from 71.7% to 83.3% (+11.7 points; 95% source-case bootstrap interval +1.7 to +21.7); in the GPT-OSS-120B set, SpeciTeller ranking raises direction-valid selection from 51.7% to 56.7% (+5.0 points; 95% source-case bootstrap interval -6.7 to +16.7), and every primary single-score GPT-OSS-120B interval includes zero. These findings tie score interpretation and decision value to the predictor and candidate set.

title: A cautionary tale on the cost-effectiveness of collaborative AI in real-world medical applications
abstract: Abstract Federated learning (FL) has gained wide popularity as a collaborative learning paradigm allowing collaborative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in sensitive healthcare applications. Nevertheless, the practical implementation of FL presents technical and organizational challenges, as it generally requires complex communication infrastructures. In this context, consensus-based learning (CBL) may represent a promising alternative for collaborative learning, allowing the combination of local knowledge into a federated decision system, while potentially reducing deployment overhead. Nevertheless, a comprehensive assessment of the viability of consensus-based learning as a cost-effective and sustainable alternative to federated learning has not yet been conducted. In this work we propose an extensive benchmark of the accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability of a panel of FL and CBL methods in a wide range of collaborative medical data analysis scenarios. The benchmark includes 7 different medical datasets, encompassing 3 machine learning tasks, 8 different data modalities, and multi-centric settings involving 3 to 23 clients. Our results reveal that CBL is a cost-effective and more sustainable alternative to FL. When compared across the panel of medical datasets in the considered benchmark, CBL methods provide equivalent accuracy to the one achieved by FL. Nonetheless, CBL significantly reduces training time and communication cost (resp. 15 fold and 131 fold decrease) ( p -value< 0.05). This study opens a novel perspective on the deployment of collaborative AI in real-world applications, whereas the adoption of cost-effective methods is instrumental to achieve sustainability and democratization of AI by alleviating the need for extensive computational resources.

title: De Wolfram Mathematica a Python: Visualización dinámica del crecimiento poblacional como estrategia de aprendizaje
abstract: The article presents a comparative analysis of how interactive simulation helps in understanding the logistic model of population growth. When teaching solely with static formulas, students face difficulties in grasping abstract concepts such as intrinsic growth rate and carrying capacity. To address this, the research evaluates two software packages: Wolfram Mathematica and Python. Methodologically, interactive simulations were implemented under a "predict-observe-explain" instructional framework, and the results were assessed across three key dimensions: the required learning curve, the flexibility to customize the environment, and the tool’s ability to foster active learning. On one hand, Wolfram allows users to build graphical interfaces quickly, but it operates under a "black box" pedagogical paradigm that hides computational processes from students and relies on expensive commercial licenses. On the other hand, Python, using open-source tools like Jupyter Notebook, presents a steeper initial learning curve. Nonetheless, it promotes active learning by requiring students to break down the model, program mathematical libraries, and understand the logic behind the simulation. The results show that both Python and Wolfram Mathematica offer flexibility, allowing the integration of theoretical narratives, executable code, and complex interactive panels (such as multispecies simulations to observe population collapse) in a single environment. The study concludes that dynamic visualization is far more effective than static pedagogical methods. The transition to Python is recommended, as it not only facilitates the teaching of dynamic systems in a virtually cost-free manner, but also enhances digital literacy and democratizes scientific knowledge by removing economic barriers in STEM (an acronym for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) education .

title: Optical Computing with Spectrally Multiplexed Features in Complex Media
abstract: Machine learning has rapidly evolved into critical technology. However, electrical hardware struggles to keep pace with the exponential growth of machine learning models. Free space optical hardware provides complementary approaches for large-scale in-memory computing, with applications across diverse machine learning tasks. Here, we explore the use of broadband light scattering in free-space optical components, specifically complex media, which generate uncorrelated optical features at each wavelength. By treating individual wavelengths as independent predictors, we demonstrate improved classification accuracy through in-silico majority voting, along with the ability to estimate uncertainty without requiring access to the model's probability outputs. We further demonstrate that linearly combining multiwavelength features, akin to spectral shaping, enables us to tune output features with improved performance on classification tasks. These advantages of optical multiplexing pave the way for more versatile system designs and broader applications of free-space optical computing system.

title: 2025–2026 Enterprise Service Management & AI Support Benchmark Report: Ticket Deflection, Resolution Latency, and Regulatory Controls in Regulated Verticals
abstract: This report synthesises published performance data for AI-assisted service operations across two functional domains — external customer support and internal enterprise service management (ESM) — and situates those data against the regulatory controls that govern banking, insurance and ecommerce operators. The primary quantitative source is the Freshservice Benchmark Report 2025, which Freshworks Inc. reports as drawing on more than 187 million tickets from 10,743 organisations in 118 countries. Within that dataset, Freshworks reports a 65.7% ticket deflection rate for its autonomous agent (Freddy AI Agent), a 76.6% reduction in average resolution time and a 41.1% improvement in first response time for agent-assist users (Freddy AI Copilot), an overall satisfaction score of 97.83%, and first-contact resolution of 74.14% for IT teams and 79.5% for business teams. Six vendor-published case studies spanning retail, financial services and enterprise ESM report deflection rates between 23% and 65% and resolution-time reductions between 25% and 73%. These figures are contextualised with public statistics on seasonal ecommerce demand, consumer-finance complaint volumes and incident-reporting deadlines. The report then maps the attestation and certification evidence available for the same platforms against those regulatory requirements, identifying two scope boundaries of practical consequence: PCI DSS coverage limited to enterprise-tier plans, and AI data-handling commitments that exclude recently acquired products. All product performance figures are vendor-reported and were not independently reproduced. Competing interests: Freshworks Inc., the maker of Freshdesk and Freshservice, is a paying client of Cllimber.

Every code embeds explicit lowest-weight X and Z logical operator witnesses, verified CSS commutativity (Hx Hz^T = 0 mod 2), pre-registration manifest, campaign spec, execution ledger journals, summary, and SHA256 checksums. 3. Key Empirical Results & Null Findings (H_{0,1}) Screened 54 codes over 44 non-abelian metacyclic groups ZSZ(l1, l2, q) across check weights w ≤ 8 and w ≤ 6. Exactly 50 codes passed all gates and non-duplication tests. Across all 50 codes, 0 advanced the public Pareto frontier. title: TITAN v2: An Empirical Adversarial Evaluation of the NEW-CIPHER v0.1 Block Cipher Under Correct Use, ECB-Style Use, and Nonce-Reuse Misuse
abstract: This paper specifies a new 128-bit block cipher, NEW-CIPHER v0.1, and reports an empirical evaluation of it with TITAN v2, a 42-test adversarial diagnostic suite. NEW-CIPHER follows the wide-trail substitution-permutation design of AES but uses its own public parameters: a field polynomial (0x15F), S-box affine layer and MDS mixing matrix circ(12, 18, 1, 1), selected by a transparent rule from counts of the Tamil script. Its S-box attains differential uniformity 4, nonlinearity 112 and algebraic degree 7, and its MixColumns matrix is MDS, so any four rounds contain at least 25 active S-boxes. The cipher uses a 256-bit key, 14 rounds and a non-linear Feistel key schedule, and is used in an authenticated mode (CTR + HMAC-SHA256, Encrypt-then-MAC). TITAN v2 assigns every diagnostic a p-value and fails it only when p < 0.001 (Bonferroni-corrected for internal multiplicity). The suite was first calibrated on an ideal keyed random function: across 40 independent runs, 4 of 1,680 diagnostics failed (0.24%). Three configurations of NEW-CIPHER were then evaluated: (A) authenticated encryption with a fresh random nonce, (B) the bare block cipher in ECB mode as a negative control, and (C) deliberate nonce reuse. Configuration A passed all 42 diagnostics in the reported run and, across 40 further runs, failed 2 of 1,680 diagnostics (0.12%), a rate indistinguishable from the ideal reference. Configurations B and C, and two weak reference ciphers (repeating-key XOR and Caesar), produced large, characteristic failures (p < 10^-12). The results are empirical evidence under stated conditions; they are not a proof of security. Code, test vectors and raw results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23073251

title: Peering inside the 'Black Box': understanding and refining deep neural networks with representational similarity analysis
abstract: Deep neural networks, and Transformer models in particular, have achieved unprecedented success in natural language processing tasks. Despite this success, they are infamous for their status as black boxes. Specific details on how they encode and process high-level linguistic task-relevant information remain difficult to characterise by humans. This hinders trust and reliability, particularly in critical applications like clinical text processing. This thesis seeks to tackle the interpretability problem by applying analytic methods inspired by cognitive science, with the overall goal to build a deeper understanding of how these models represent and process language, and suggest model interventions based on these findings. Two primary research questions guide this investigation: how do Transformer models represent and process linguistic features, and how do variations in model architecture, training data, or fine-tuning influence these representations? The thesis comprises varied technical chapters with a motivational thread of linguistic interpretability. The work begins with an exploration into interpretability within the clinical domain, developing a perturbative technique to identify diagnostically influential sentences in clinical letters. I then transition to more advanced interpretability techniques, introducing Representational Similarity Analysis and linear probing. A particular focus is placed on layer-wise analysis to observe how salient linguistic signals are encoded throughout the network. Expanding on this, I use these techniques to measure the fine-grained representation of noun-noun compound thematic relations. This toolkit is then applied to Irish morphosyntax, comparing monolingual and multilingual models to demonstrate the monolingual model's stronger encoding of specific linguistic phenomena. Finally, I introduce Representational Similarity Regularisation, a novel approach to inducing alignment between representations and a target signal. This method aligns models with cognitive signals elicited by natural language, improving performance on semantic textual similarity tasks. This thesis provides novel insights into Transformer models and explores using cognitive signals to build more robust human-aligned neural networks.

evidence.title: Peering inside the 'Black Box': understanding and refining deep neural networks with representational similarity analysis
evidence.abstract: Deep neural networks, and Transformer models in particular, have achieved unprecedented success in natural language processing tasks. Despite this success, they are infamous for their status as black boxes. Specific details on how they encode and process high-level linguistic task-relevant information remain difficult to characterise by humans. This hinders trust and reliability, particularly in critical applications like clinical text processing. This thesis seeks to tackle the interpretability problem by applying analytic methods inspired by cognitive science, with the overall goal to build a deeper understanding of how these models represent and process language, and suggest model interventions based on these findings. Two primary research questions guide this investigation: how do Transformer models represent and process linguistic features, and how do variations in model architecture, training data, or fine-tuning influence these representations? The thesis comprises varied technical chapters with a motivational thread of linguistic interpretability. The work begins with an exploration into interpretability within the clinical domain, developing a perturbative technique to identify diagnostically influential sentences in clinical letters. I then transition to more advanced interpretability techniques, introducing Representational Similarity Analysis and linear probing. A particular focus is placed on layer-wise analysis to observe how salient linguistic signals are encoded throughout the network. Expanding on this, I use these techniques to measure the fine-grained representation of noun-noun compound thematic relations. This toolkit is then applied to Irish morphosyntax, comparing monolingual and multilingual models to demonstrate the monolingual model's stronger encoding of specific linguistic phenomena. Finally, I introduce Representational Similarity Regularisation, a novel approach to inducing alignment between representations and a target signal. This method aligns models with cognitive signals elicited by natural language, improving performance on semantic textual similarity tasks. This thesis provides novel insights into Transformer models and explores using cognitive signals to build more robust human-aligned neural networks.

title: TARGET: A Text-Anchored Gated Enhancement Transformer for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) benefits from complementary textual, acoustic, and visual cues, yet effectively exploiting weak non-textual evidence remains challenging for fine-grained sentiment recognition. Existing language-centric methods mainly strengthen cross-modal interaction, but provide limited control over the complete pathway through which auxiliary evidence is selected, aligned, accumulated, and finally allowed to modify the textual representation. As a result, local redundancy, cross-modal discrepancy, and uncontrolled information injection may obscure subtle sentiment-intensity differences.To address this problem, we propose TARGET, a Text-Anchored Gated Enhancement Transformer that treats text as a persistent semantic anchor throughout multimodal evidence integration. Rather than stacking independent fusion modules, TARGET organizes multimodal processing as a sequential evidence-control pipeline. A text-anchored low-rank Rényi entropy-based Information Bottleneck first refines noisy and redundant modality-specific information before fusion. Contrastive Self-Alignment then regularizes the refined cross-modal interface while preserving complementary modality-specific cues. Finally, Text-Anchored Cross-Modal Interaction progressively constructs a text-aligned global evidence stream through a Hierarchical Shell Structure and selectively updates the textual state through Gated Global Semantic Injection.Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS demonstrate competitive overall performance and particularly strong fine-grained sentiment recognition, while extensive ablation and diagnostic analyses verify the complementary roles of the proposed stages. These results suggest that controlling the lifecycle of auxiliary evidence, rather than merely increasing cross-modal interaction, provides an effective paradigm for fine-grained multimodal sentiment modeling and offers a promising basis for more reliable and adaptive multimodal affective systems.

title: Does Every User Need a Private LoRA? Decoupling Personalization from Per-User Adaptation
abstract: Personalized large language models often require a complete adaptation state for each user. However, this paradigm scales poorly as the user population grows. We revisit this design through the lens of personalization capacity allocation: how much adaptation capacity can be shared across users, how the shared capacity should be composed, and how much must remain user-specific. We answer them through three complementary empirical analyses. We find that independent user adapters contain substantial cross-user reusable structure, that the utility of reusable directions reflects both user relevance and variation across queries, and that user histories provide transferable signals for compact individual correction. Motivated by these findings, we propose LINEUP. It learns a bank of reusable low-rank personalization factors, composes them through user-conditioned recall and query-dependent calibration, and restricts target-user adaptation to a tiny user code over a shared correction space. This design decouples expressive personalization capacity from per-user trainable state. Each target user optimizes only eight scalars, while all shared components remain fixed. By comparison, the evaluated private-LoRA configuration uses 4.19 million per-user parameters. Our theoretical analysis gives a finite-step, finite-history risk bound and sufficient conditions for user-code refinement to improve on history initialization. Across six tasks spanning personalized classification, prediction, and generation, LINEUP leads on all 12 metrics, each averaged over three independent runs (e.g., reducing LaMP-3 RMSE by 11.4% relative to the strongest baseline). It maintains advantages under limited history. These results show that rich personalization can be supported primarily by reusable, conditionally composed shared capacity, while independent user adaptation remains confined to a tiny correction state.

title: What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language
abstract: Difficulty is one of the most fundamental properties of a question: it determines whether the question can meaningfully discriminate between models of differing ability. Although a variety of methods can now estimate or predict difficulty automatically, they yield only a single descriptive number, with no account of the underlying factors that make a question difficult in the first place. In this work, we propose a data-driven approach that automatically generates and validates natural-language hypotheses explaining what makes one question harder than another. We first estimate each item's difficulty from the responses of a large pool of LLMs using Item Response Theory. We then sample contrasting sets of easy and hard questions and prompt an LLM to propose candidate explanations of the difference, which are subsequently validated and selected on held-out questions. Experimental results across three datasets spanning mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning show that our method produces interpretable and predictive hypotheses. On their own, they predict the difficulty of unseen questions competitively with, or better than, advanced black-box difficulty regressors; used as additional features, they further improve those regressors, implying that they discover difficulty signals that existing models fail to capture. Moreover, we demonstrate that editing questions according to a hypothesis can shift their measured difficulty in the expected direction, indicating that the discovered hypotheses are causally valid difficulty factors rather than post-hoc descriptions. Our approach thus turns a purely descriptive difficulty score into actionable statements.

title: Agents Are Systems, Not Models: Rethinking Agentic Evaluation
abstract: Agent evaluations increasingly go beyond a single success rate, reporting metrics such as cost, consistency, and robustness. Yet they typically treat the agent itself as fixed. In practice, an agent is a configurable system: users decide what to tell it, how long to let it run, and which model to use, and each of these choices can change how well and how consistently it performs. We study these choices on a new benchmark of four scientific tasks, where a coding agent must find and correctly operate a published specialist model. We investigate five parts of the agent's configuration: task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model. We find substantial run-to-run variability, with approximately 54% of the outcome variance coming from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it. Across configurations, the information provided to the agent has the largest effect, exceeding both time budget and model size, while also reducing cost and improving calibration. Configuration choices also interact: additional time helps only when the agent has sufficient information or a capable enough model to use it. Finally, a trajectory-based taxonomy of agent behavior reveals that prompting an agent to verify its answer has little effect on its verification behavior, whereas providing a dedicated verification tool changes that behavior substantially. These results suggest that agents should be evaluated as configurable systems themselves, and that some desired behaviors are more effectively implemented in the system than requested through prompting. We release the benchmark and more than 18,000 agent trajectories.

title: Decision Titan: Test-Time Training for Long-Term Memory in Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Long-term dependencies remain a major challenge for sequential decision-making in the field of AI: RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients and the limited expressivity of vector-based hidden states, whilst Transformer-based models are limited by the quadratic scaling of attention. Recent work has proposed tackling this problem with the Test-Time Training (TTT) framework, which stores episodic memories in the parameters of a neural network through gradient descent at both train and test-time. This approach has seen success in the domain of Natural Language Processing, however, to the best of our knowledge it has not yet been applied to the domain of Reinforcement Learning (RL), nor has there been a study analysing how this memory practically functions. In this paper, we study the potential of the TTT framework for offline RL by augmenting a Decision Transformer with TTT layers, dubbed the Decision Titan. We analyse performance and properties of the model in the X-Maze environment, an extension of T-Maze designed to test sequential memory, and investigate how the memory mechanism learns by visualising gate values over time. Our key findings are that Decision Titan can learn long-term dependencies with ranges 20x longer than the context window, generalises to lengths 1.7x the training data, but crucially temporal generalisation depends on the time embeddings used, and the ability to learn long-term dependencies depends on how the relevant information is encoded.

title: Optimal Transport Meets Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently compare probability distributions, such as state visitation distributions induced by policies and experts, action distributions from learned policies and offline datasets, or transition distributions from learned models and environments. However, commonly used divergences may become ineffective when these distributions overlap weakly, which is frequently encountered in imitation learning, offline RL, and deployment under distribution shift. Optimal transport (OT) offers an alternative by measuring the cost of \emph{moving} probability mass from one distribution to another under a ground cost that encodes task geometry. This survey covers how OT is used inside RL objectives and algorithms. For each method, we identify: the role OT plays, the distributions compared, the OT formulation used, and the treatment of temporal structure. Beyond categorising existing methods, we discuss the motivations behind different OT choices, practical considerations such as cost design and computational challenges, and highlight open problems including scalable trajectory-level transport, principled handling of mass mismatch, and theoretical analysis for OT-regularised RL.

title: Modeling Shipping Emissions: Machine Learning, Engineering, and Policy Counterfactuals
abstract: Machine learning predicts outcomes well, but predictive accuracy does not ensure reliable counterfactual responses. We examine how to combine machine learning and theory for measurement and counterfactual analysis, using maritime CO2 emissions where physics provides a benchmark speed response. Matching hourly tracking data for dry bulk and container ships to annual fuel consumption reported under EU regulations, we compare engineering calculations, structural regressions, hybrid models, and machine learning. Out of sample, all estimated models predict within a few percent of reported totals, outperforming standard engineering calculations. Yet pure machine learning and unrestricted structural regression imply attenuated speed responses. Hybrids preserve the structural component's speed response by excluding speed-related inputs from the machine learning component. A cost-benefit analysis of speed reductions illustrates the policy stakes: an attenuated speed response can flip the sign of net benefits. Accurate aggregate predictions therefore cannot substitute for scrutiny of the restrictions determining counterfactual responses.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Risk Assessment in Developmental Toxicity Studies With Ordinal Responses
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a nonparametric Bayesian modeling framework for clustered ordinal responses in developmental toxicity studies, which typically exhibit extensive heterogeneity. The primary focus of these studies is to examine dose–response relationships, which are depicted by (conditional) endpoint probabilities across the dose (toxin) levels. Standard parametric approaches, limited in terms of the response distribution and/or the dose–response relationship, hinder reliable uncertainty quantification in this context. We propose nonparametric mixture models that are built from dose‐dependent stick‐breaking process priors, leveraging the continuation‐ratio logits representation of the multinomial distribution to formulate the mixture kernel. We further elaborate the modeling approach, amplifying the mixture models with an overdispersed kernel which offers enhanced control of variability. We conduct a simulation study to demonstrate the uncertainty quantification benefits of both the discrete nonparametric mixing structure and the overdispersed kernel. Further illustration is provided with different forms of risk assessment, using data from a toxicity experiment on the effects of ethylene glycol.

title: WHEN VIRTUAL WORLDS BECOME INTELLIGENT
abstract: The recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have contributed to a significant visibility of generative AI. Despite the big spotlights being on AI nowadays, the ambition to develop computational systems capable of creating the illusion of intelligent behaviour is not new. One can date AI to the 1950s, when various researchers raised the topic and made remarkable contributions to the field’s establishment and evolution.

title: Ukrainian Frequency: word stress for every lemma of the top-12,000 list (over ukrainian-word-stress, en.wiktionary and uk.wiktionary)
abstract: A stressed form for each of the 12,000 lemma-and-part-of-speech rows of the Ukrainian Frequency list (v0.2.0, over UberText 2.0), keyed on the list's ranks: one confident stress where the open sources agree (9,674 of the 9,920 polysyllabic common words, 97.5 percent), a labeled free variant, homograph or dictionary-only doublet where they do not (225), and an honest `missing` for the 21 rows no source resolved. The 1,348 proper nouns are out of scope by owner decision: kept on their rows with the stress the pipeline found and the pipeline's status in the note, counted in no share. Every row carries the provenance of its stress; every manual decision is a ledgered override. Current release v1.0.0, CC-BY-SA 4.0 because of the Wiktionary-derived rows; kept as its own file rather than a column on the CC-BY list so the list is not relicensed. Reviewed snapshot of 2026-10-01 over list v0.2.0: ukrainian-word-stress 2.1.0 read directly from its trie and filtered by the list's UD part of speech, en.wiktionary (kaikki.org) and uk.wiktionary (dump) for doublets, a two-of-three vote, 19 goroh.pp.ua tiebreaks recorded as attested stress only, uk.wikipedia leads for 116 names, and a manual-decision ledger applied last. Joined on rank; kept as its own CC-BY-SA file so the CC-BY list is not relicensed. v1.0.1 (2026-10-07) corrects the credit for ukrainian-word-stress in the README and datasheet (a lang-uk project by Oleksiy Syvokon, maintained by Dmytro Chaplynskyi); the data files are byte-identical to v1.0.0. Datasheet, attribution and known defects: DATASHEET.md in this record. Checksums: manifest.json. Live page: https://www.jakelawrence.xyz/research/ukrainian-frequency.

title: A Deterministic Gate for Containing Prompt-Induced Unauthorized Record Updates (M-Anchor App V1)
abstract: M-Anchor App is a local Python application that separates AI-generated proposals from authoritative case-record updates. A deterministic gate checks the referenced state, externally admitted evidence, candidate transitions, and authority requests before saving a change. Its principle is: Model proposes; deterministic layer commits. The V1 demonstration includes four fixed attack types (unsupported resolution, forged evidence admission, future-check bypass, and state-reference tampering), two controls, an optional model connection, and separate English and Japanese documentation with a bilingual interface. Input, proposal, decision, and read-back state can be inspected and exported. The source package includes reproduction instructions, validation records, and two original observation exports containing 20 entries and one entry, respectively. The fixed observations show rejection of four invalid proposal types and acceptance of a supported update. Three model-route observations record one adversarial input that the model itself answered by preserving uncertainty, one valid no-change proposal, and one supported update saved from Version 1 to Version 2. The adversarial model example is not a gate rejection of an invalid model output. “Attack neutralization” is limited here to blocking unauthorized case-record transitions at the gate. The app does not prevent all incorrect GPT text, establish evidence truth, control external tools, or demonstrate universal prompt-injection or jailbreak resistance. This is a software demonstration with inspectable evidence, not an independently certified security product. Python 3.10 or later is required; fixed scenarios need no model API key. This distribution is licensed under Apache-2.0, permitting commercial use, modification, and redistribution under its terms. The M-Anchor Framework is a related, separately versioned project.

title: Whole-Path Hit Rates and Error in Sparse Range–Bearing Forecasting: research data, code and manuscript
abstract: Access update (1 October 2026): The authors have restricted file access for journal peer review. Record metadata and DOI remain public. Editors and reviewers may access the files using a private read-only link supplied separately through the journal submission system. This record was briefly publicly accessible before the restriction. Public-format correction: the manuscript and supplement now use a neutral standard LaTeX article layout. Scientific text, figures, tables, results and research evidence archive bytes are unchanged from v17-final (10.5281/zenodo.23073421). This version supersedes the template-formatted public documents. Research archive accompanying Whole-Path Hit Rates and Error in Sparse Range–Bearing Forecasting (v17-neutral), by Xu Zhang and Xianjian Zhang. The package includes the manuscript and supplement, multi-file LaTeX source, synthetic observations, model checkpoints, original evaluation records, observation-only replay, and separately labelled post-review extensions. title: Structural Barriers to the Deployment of AI Foundation Models
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) foundation models excel at benchmarks but are not always cost-effective or successfully deployed in enterprise systems. This paper analyzes the failures in their deployment through interconnected structural components characterized by: Economic constraints (computational costs, memory, and latency that scale with increasing use of AI model services), cognitive constraints (related to training objectives that optimize plausibility rather than causal reasoning and calibrated uncertainty), and socio-technical constraints (requirements for organizational change, accountability, and governance). The study examines why the deployment of AI models in real-world enterprise environments remains difficult. It focuses on four themes – scalability, reliability, interpretability, and practical deployment – aiming to demonstrate why these problems do not disappear even as models improve, and how these issues reinforce each other, thereby leading to higher costs and greater risk. In conclusion, the study outlines alternative development pathways, including the use of alternative architectural paradigms such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), hybrid Neuro-symbolic AI, compound and multi-agent systems, and human-in-the-loop designs, which may offer more practical and sustainable ways to align foundation models with the organizational, operational, and governance requirements of the enterprise environment. Additionally, a four-dimensional framework is proposed for assessing a model’s deployment readiness based on economic viability, reliability and safety, auditability, and organizational readiness.

title: DEEP NEURAL NETWORK-BASED SPEAKER AUTHENTICATION FOR SECURE ACCESS CONTROL SYSTEMS
abstract: In the digital age, the importance of biometric identification technologies is increasing due to the increasing demand for reliable, secure, and user-friendly access control systems for electronic devices. One of the promising areas of such technologies is speaker authentication, which allows confirming identity based on a person’s unique voice characteristics. However, traditional methods cannot provide the required level of stability in different acoustic environments, background noise conditions, and changes in speech features. In the presented research work, a comprehensive approach is proposed that combines multi-frequency coefficients (MFCCs), x-vector-based speaker inputs, and deep neural networks (DNNs) to improve the accuracy and stability of speaker authentication. The proposed architecture consists of preprocessing speech signals, extracting MFCC features, forming x-vector inputs, and classifying speakers using DNN. An experimental dataset consisting of audio recordings of 100 speakers was used to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model. As a result of the experiment, the proposed model achieved 98.5% authentication accuracy, 99.4% precision, 97.6% recall, and a 98.5% F1-score. In addition, the false acceptance rate (FAR) was 0.6%, the false rejection rate (FRR) was 2.4%, and the equal error rate (EER) was approximately 1.5%. These results indicate that the model can distinguish between authorized and unauthorized users with high accuracy. The proposed approach showed superior results compared to traditional machine learning and deep learning models, which proved the effectiveness of combining acoustic features and deep speaker embeddings. The results indicate that the proposed method can be used in secure access control to electronic devices, biometric user identification, and voice authentication systems.

title: Objects and Classes Will Do
abstract: Objects and classes were introduced by SIMULA some sixty years ago. Since then, many new language mechanisms have been devised including static members, namespaces, modules, companion objects, interfaces, mixins, traits, protocols, constructors, factories, iterators, etc. The implications are that many languages have become complex entities with many rules, special cases, and exceptions to the rules, often due to lack of uniformity and generality.

title: SKC-Net: A Standard-Cell Key-Feature Contrastive-Learning network for cervical abnormal cell detection
abstract: Deep learning-based detection of abnormal cells in cervical ThinPrep Cytology Test images represents a pivotal advancement in intelligent cervical cancer screening systems. In this context, the effective utilization of standard cell features in images is paramount.On one hand, the TBS diagnostic criteria delineate the differentiation based on feature comparisons between normal and abnormal cells. On the other hand, signiffcant inter-sample variations can lead to confusion during the learning process in conventional object detection networks. To mimic the diagnostic reasoning of professional pathologists, this paper introduces the Standard-Cell Key-Feature Contrastive-Learning Network for detecting cervical abnormal cells. The network initially extracts key features from both standard and abnormal cells and effectively aligns them using consistency-guided contrastive loss. To better distinguish the unique characteristics of standard and abnormal cells, we have designed a Multi-Color-Domain Convolution Module and an Adaptive Contour Approximation Module, which are based on TBS diagnostic criteria—focusing respectively on the preliminary extraction of color and shape features. Furthermore, to mitigate information loss during deep feature learning, we propose a Dual-Branch Differentiated Convolution Module aimed at enhancing the model’s learning capacity and memory retention. Finally, to guide the model’s learning process by leveraging standard cell key features, we introduce the Cell Instance-Level Contrastive Supervision Module; this enhancement signiffcantly boosts the overall model performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method improves the mean Average Precision by 3.4% and 3.0% on the CLBC and CRIC datasets,respectively, achieving scores of 65.2% and 71.8%.These findings underscore the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

title: Training datasets tailored for domain-specific large language models: challenges, methods and trends
abstract: Adapting LLMs to specialized domains critically depends on high-quality training data, making dataset construction a decisive factor in domain performance. This survey reviews methods for constructing domain-adaptation training datasets through a structured, data-centric analysis. Based on a comparative analysis of representative domain-specific LLMs, we organize the literature around three technical dimensions that address limited data availability, heterogeneous quality and inefficient utilization: data synthesis , data selection and data composition . For data synthesis, we examine paradigms based on instruction rewriting, unlabeled-corpus reconstruction, retrieval augmentation and knowledge-graph-guided generation. For data selection, we trace the progression from heuristic rule-based filtering to model-aware methods that estimate sample quality and training utility. Data composition encompasses mechanisms that control the effective training-data distribution by determining which data are used, how strongly different data contribute to optimization and when each data type is introduced. We further examine catastrophic forgetting during domain adaptation and summarize data-centric mitigation strategies based on replay, mixture design, data ordering and stage-wise allocation. Overall, this survey provides a systematic reference for constructing domain-adaptation training datasets and supports the transition of LLMs from general-purpose foundation models to domain-specialized systems.

title: Unifying Privacy Accounting: Information Equivalence and Information Loss
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) admits several notions, but the choice among them may affect both privacy analysis and utility. In this paper, we consider four mainstream curve-based privacy notions within a unified information-theoretic framework. For a fixed ordered pair of output distributions, we establish information equivalence among the two directional privacy profiles of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP, the pair of hypothesis-testing trade-off functions, and the extended privacy-loss distribution. The exact Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve joins this equivalence class whenever it is finite at some order greater than one. Under this mild condition, choosing among these notions changes only their semantic interpretation and computational requirements. In contrast, taking the maximum of the directional privacy profiles or compressing the RDP curve into a single zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) parameter can lose information. We quantify the information loss between the exact RDP curve and its zCDP bound for standard noise mechanisms. This gap is zero for Gaussian noise but generally positive for Gaussian-mixture, Laplace, discrete Gaussian, and Poisson-subsampled Gaussian mechanisms. Moreover, this gap grows linearly with the number of independently composed mechanisms. Our information-theoretic perspective has practical consequences. At the same certified privacy level, retaining the full RDP curve rather than using zCDP reduces the required noise variance by up to $45\%$ for Gaussian-mixture noise in workloads comparable in size to the American Community Survey. For DP-SGD on Fashion-MNIST under Poisson subsampling, an RDP-based privacy accountant improves test accuracy by up to $8.73$ percentage points compared to a zCDP-based accountant when both are calibrated to the same $(\varepsilon,δ)$ guarantee.

title: Invertibility of structured perturbations of singular matrices over unital rings
abstract: In this article, we study the invertibility of matrices of the form A+EDF, where A and D are square matrices over a unital, not necessarily commutative, ring and A is singular. Under natural hypotheses on kernels and images, we prove that A+EDF is invertible if and only if D is invertible, and obtain an explicit formula for the inverse of A+EDF by purely algebraic methods. When the coefficient ring is stably finite, or more specifically a field, we obtain an invertibility criterion under weaker hypotheses. Our results extend and sharpen a theorem of Eriksson and Nordqvist for complex matrices.

title: Teaching LLMs to Hear Who Spoke What: Metadata-Supervised Pretraining for Encoder-Free Speech-LLMs
abstract: Encoder-based speech large language models (Speech-LLMs) commonly employ pretrained speech encoders that prioritize linguistic content but may discard fine-grained acoustic cues essential for speaker discrimination and paralinguistic understanding. Encoder-free Speech-LLMs instead map Mel-spectrogram features directly into the LLM input space through lightweight embedding layers, enabling the LLM to learn from low-level acoustic features. However, systematic pretraining strategies for encoder-free Speech-LLMs remain underexplored, limiting their ability to compensate for the absence of large-scale pretrained speech encoders. We propose metadata-supervised pretraining (MSP), which leverages speech attributes such as speaker identity and emotion to develop speaker-discriminative and paralinguistic capabilities. We further introduce speaker-aware utterance composition (SAUC) to strengthen speaker discrimination and apply random span masking to regularize pretraining. We primarily evaluate our approach on joint ASR and speaker diarization in multi-speaker conversations, complemented by experiments on paralinguistic speech-understanding tasks. Under matched training-data conditions, our encoder-free model outperforms its randomly initialized encoder-based counterpart. With limited metadata-annotated data, it is competitive with models using speech encoders pretrained on substantially larger corpora, outperforming them in several settings. These results demonstrate the potential of encoder-free architectures for building native multimodal LLMs that acquire diverse speech capabilities.

title: Efficient learning of quantum interactions from thermal metastable states
abstract: Learning quantum interactions from finite-temperature many-body systems is a central task in emerging quantum platforms. Recently, the problem of learning from lattice quantum Gibbs states has found rigorous, efficient protocols. Nevertheless, exact Gibbs states, as the input premise, are in fact computationally intractable to prepare and may not faithfully represent generic finite-temperature quantum systems. In contrast, a system coupled to a heat bath can be stuck at an approximate stationary state (metastable state) long before it truly equilibrates. Here, we formulate a physically and algorithmically consistent alternative: learning from such metastable states of detailed-balanced master equations (Lindbladians) arising from system-bath interactions. We distill the algorithmic mechanism and structural condition underlying Gibbs-state learning and extend it in full to metastable states, attaining nearly optimal sample and computational complexity (in the system size and the precision). More broadly, we sharpen notions of metastability and develop a unified framework for finite-temperature learning.

title: Zero- Versus Infinite-Temperature Damping in Variational Quantum Circuits: Feature Scale, Sampling Cost, and Frame Gauge
abstract: The Pauli twirl of amplitude damping (AD) is generalized amplitude damping at infinite temperature: it keeps the contraction of AD and removes its non-unital term, so comparing the two in variational circuits isolates the zero-temperature bias, which acts mainly through the scale of the features. For random parameters, features under AD settle on a floor, which at strong damping is set by the last layer, has a closed form, and at fixed $T_1$ falls with temperature as $\tanh(\hbarω/2k_BT)$; under the twirls they shrink by a constant factor per layer, up to eight qubits. A trainable output scale removes most of the resulting accuracy differences, leaving AD ahead of its twirls by at most about three percentage points in our simulations; what it removes reappears as a cost in measurement shots: trained and tested with $10^3$ shots per image, a four-qubit classifier under AD at $p=0.3$ stays within 1.5 points of noiseless accuracy, while the twirled classifiers lose up to 33. At weaker damping the separation depth grows roughly as $(np)^{-1}\ln(1/p)$. The damping direction is a gauge when the damping follows complete entangling layers and the circuit boundaries are trainable; in an eigensolver it becomes physical inside a decomposed two-qubit gate.
